The Prairie vole (Microtus ochrogaster) is a small arvicoline rodent widely distributed across the grasslands of central North America, where it serves as a key prey species for raptors and mammalian carnivores. Neonates emerge from the birth canal weighing an average of 3.02 grams [Wwb = 3.02 grams], a mass that reflects the altricial state of the newborn pups at parturition. Adult body size exhibits limited sexual dimorphism, with field-captured individuals attaining an ultimate wet weight of 40 grams [Wwi = 40 grams] under optimal forage conditions, though considerable geographic variation exists. This modest body mass places Microtus ochrogaster among the smaller members of its genus, a trait that influences its high surface-to-volume ratio and, consequently, its thermoregulatory demands. The species is renowned in life-history circles for its rapid maturation rate and high fecundity, which are typical of the r-selected strategy observed in many grassland microtines. Under standard laboratory conditions maintained at 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C], captivity records indicate that females reach sexual maturity after a remarkably short interval, with time since birth at puberty for female being 47 days [tp = 47 days], an adaptation that allows populations to rebound quickly following crash events.

Females are capable of producing multiple litters annually, and extrapolations from captive colony data suggest a maximum reproductive rate of approximately 4 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 4 litters per year]. This combined reproductive strategy—a moderate litter size coupled with frequent breeding bouts—enables populations to achieve explosive growth during periods of abundant grass and forb cover. At a uniform thermal regime of 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C], nutritional independence marks a critical transition in the life cycle, occurring at time since birth at weaning of 20 days [tx = 20 days]. At this juncture, the young voles have reached a wet weight at weaning of 16.7 grams [Wwx = 16.7 grams], representing a more than five-fold increase from their neonatal mass of 3.02 grams [Wwb = 3.02 grams] and reflecting an extraordinarily rapid period of somatic growth. The newly weaned juveniles disperse from the natal nest to establish their own home ranges, a behavior that reduces competition among siblings.
